title: Dead Letter Queues and Poison-Message Handling
lesson:
When a consumer pulls a message off a queue and fails to process it, most messaging systems make the message visible again so it can be retried. That is the right behavior for transient failures, but some messages fail every single time: a malformed payload, a bug in the handler, a reference to a record that no longer exists, or an event in a schema version the consumer does not understand. These are called poison messages. Redelivering them forever wastes CPU and I/O, inflates error metrics, and — in an ordered or low-concurrency queue — blocks every healthy message stuck behind them. A dead letter queue (DLQ) is a separate queue the broker routes a message to after it has failed too many times (or expired, or exceeded a size limit), pulling the bad message out of the main flow while preserving it for inspection instead of silently dropping it.

How a message ends up there depends on the broker. Amazon SQS uses a redrive policy: each message carries a receive count, and once it has been received more than maxReceiveCount times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the DLQ named in the policy. RabbitMQ dead-letters a message when it is rejected or nacked with requeue=false, when its per-message or per-queue TTL expires, or when the queue hits a length limit, routing it through a configured dead-letter exchange. Core Kafka has no built-in DLQ for consumer applications, so teams implement the pattern themselves: after a bounded number of failed attempts the consumer produces the record — usually annotated with the original topic, partition, offset, exception, and attempt count — to a dedicated dead letter topic and advances its offset.

A DLQ is only useful if something watches it. An unmonitored DLQ is data loss with extra bookkeeping. A healthy setup alerts on DLQ depth and arrival rate (a rising DLQ means something is broken right now), provides tooling to inspect payloads and failure reasons, and offers a redrive path to replay messages back onto the main queue once the bug is fixed or a flaky dependency recovers. It also helps to classify failures before dead-lettering: a downstream timeout is usually transient and deserves a few retries with exponential backoff and jitter, while a schema-parse error is permanent and should go to the DLQ immediately. Matching retry policy to the failure class avoids both premature dead-lettering and endless useless retries.

A few design details matter in practice. Set the retry limit high enough to ride out brief blips but low enough that a true poison message does not stall an ordered queue for long, since a stuck message at the head blocks everything behind it. Make the consumer idempotent: a message whose processing actually succeeded but whose acknowledgement was lost will be redelivered, and without idempotency it can be executed several times and then dead-lettered after already doing its work. Finally, the DLQ is itself a queue with its own retention and size limits, so monitor and drain it like any other — a DLQ that overflows or expires loses the very messages it was meant to protect.

options: A message that fails processing on every redelivery attempt, so retrying it indefinitely never succeeds
A message that has been encrypted so the consumer cannot read its body
A message that was delivered successfully but whose acknowledgement was lost
Any message that sits in the queue longer than a few seconds before being consumed
questions.explanation: A poison message is one that deterministically fails processing, so unbounded redelivery just burns resources and can stall the queue.

questions.prompt: Moving failed messages to a dead letter queue and never monitoring or draining it is an acceptable permanent resting place for them.
questions.explanation: An unwatched DLQ is just data loss with extra steps; a DLQ needs alerting on its depth, tooling to inspect payloads, and a path to replay messages once the underlying bug is fixed.

questions.prompt: In Amazon SQS, what determines when a message is moved from the main queue to its dead letter queue?
options: The redrive policy's maxReceiveCount — once a message has been received that many times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the configured DLQ
A fixed 24-hour timer that applies to every message regardless of processing outcome
The consumer explicitly publishing the message to the DLQ by name
Whenever the main queue exceeds 120,000 in-flight messages
questions.explanation: SQS tracks a receive count per message and, per the queue's redrive policy, relocates the message to the DLQ once that count exceeds maxReceiveCount.

questions.prompt: Core Kafka has no built-in dead letter queue for consumer applications, so teams typically implement one by producing a failed record to a separate dead letter ____ after a bounded number of processing attempts.
questions.explanation: In Kafka the DLQ pattern is application-level: after N failed attempts the consumer publishes the record (often with failure metadata) to a dedicated topic and moves its offset on.

questions.prompt: In a strictly ordered queue, a poison message at the head can block processing of every message behind it until that message is removed or dead-lettered.
questions.explanation: Ordering forces the consumer to finish (or give up on) the head message before advancing, so head-of-line blocking makes fast dead-lettering especially important for ordered queues.

questions.prompt: A handler can tell a downstream timeout (likely transient) apart from a schema-parse error (permanent) by the exception type. What is the sensible handling?
options: Retry the timeout a few times with exponential backoff and jitter before dead-lettering; send the parse error straight to the DLQ
Dead-letter both immediately so the queue never slows down
Retry both forever, since any failure might eventually clear
Drop both silently to keep error metrics clean
questions.explanation: Matching retry policy to the failure class avoids premature dead-lettering of recoverable errors and avoids endless retries of genuinely broken messages.

questions.prompt: Order the lifecycle of a poison message under a max-receive / redrive policy, earliest first.
items: The broker routes the message to the dead letter queue instead of redelivering it
A consumer receives the message and processing fails, so the message becomes visible again
An operator inspects the DLQ, fixes the bug, and redrives the message back to the main queue
The message's delivery count crosses the configured maximum
questions.explanation: Repeated failed deliveries increment the receive count until it exceeds the threshold, at which point the broker moves the message to the DLQ for later inspection and redrive.
